title: skill
text:
Kosha() opens two indexes, the repo index (.kosha/code.db) and the index of installed packages (kosha/env.db in the user data directory), plus the call graph over both. Check that they are current before trusting an answer, because code missing from a stale index looks the same as code that does not exist:
from kosha import Kosha
k = Kosha()
k.status()
# {'files': 4, 'packages': 355, 'graph_nodes': 10630, 'stale_files': 0, 'stale_pkgs': {'httpx': '0.28.1'}, 'new_files': 0}
Sync only when something you need is stale. Computing embeddings for changed code is the one slow step:
k.sync()                            # repo, stale packages and call graph
k.sync(embed=False)                 # store new chunks without embeddings: keyword search only, much faster
k.sync(pkgs=['httpx'], repo=False)  # one package
Then search. context is the default and searches both indexes; env_context and repo_context search one each and are faster:
for r in k.env_context('atomic file write preserving permissions', limit=8):
    print(r['metadata']['mod_name'], r['metadata'].get('lineno'), r['content'][:120])

title: skill
text:
Which call answers which question







Question
Call




Is the index current?
k.status()


Does a dependency already do this?
k.env_context('desc', limit=8)


What pattern does this codebase use?
k.context('desc', graph=True, limit=15)


Repo only, no packages
k.repo_context('desc')


Look over many hits without their source
k.context('desc', compact=True)


Who calls this, what does it call, what are its peers?
k.ni('fastcore.basics.merge')


How do two nodes connect?
k.short_path('a.fn', 'b.fn')


What is within n calls of a node?
k.neighbors('kosha.core.Kosha', depth=2)


What does a package export?
k.public_api('fastcore')


Which functions of a package does the most code depend on?
k.top_nodes('fastcore', k=5)


How does package A reach package B?
k.api_call_paths('kosha', 'litesearch')


Which packages does a package import, layer by layer?
k.dep_stack(['fastcore'], depth=2)


Where should new code go?
k.where_to_add('desc', limit=5)


Search READMEs and other prose, not code
k.docs_context('desc')



pkg_context searches package descriptions, one per indexed package, to find a package by what it does. doc(Kosha) lists every method with its signature; the table is a map, not the full reference. Indexing (update_repo, update_pkgs, process_env) and deleting (nuke, rm_pkg, prune_old_pkgs) are methods of the same class, but sync is the only one you normally need.

title: skill
text:
Filters
Filters go inside the query string, next to the plain words, and work with context, env_context and repo_context.









Token
Aliases
Example
Effect




package:
pkg:, packages:, pkgs:
package:fastcore
one package


path:
dir:, folder:, paths:
path:xtras
path contains the text


file:
filename:, files:
file:xtras*
path matches the glob


lang:
ext:, extension:, langs:
lang:py
language, by file extension


type:
types:
type:FunctionDef
kind of definition



Separate several values with commas to accept any of them (package:httpx,requests). Every filter excludes code that does not match, and a trailing ! (package!:x) means the same as without it. In context, a package: filter also skips the repo search. A package name written as a plain word, as in k.context('fastcore atomic save'), is not a filter: it ranks that package’s hits higher, and other packages still appear.
A filter-shaped token with an unknown key is reported in parseq(q)[1]['_unknown'], and the command line prints a warning. The token is searched as plain text, so a typo such as libr:litesearch would otherwise return a full page of results that ignore the filter you meant.

title: skill
text:
Reading a result
{'content':  'def merge(*ds):\n    "Merge all dicts"\n    ...',
 'metadata': {'mod_name': 'fastcore.basics.merge',   # the name to pass to ni() and short_path()
              'path': '.../fastcore/basics.py', 'lineno': 655,
              'type': 'FunctionDef', 'package': 'fastcore',
              'public_api': True, 'docstring': 'Merge all dicts'},
 'pagerank': 0.00027, 'in_degree': 8, 'out_degree': 12,
 'callers': [...], 'callees': [...], 'co_dispatched': []}
pagerank measures how much code depends on a node. Changing a node with a high score affects more code, so look at its callers first. callers shows where the code is used, and callees shows what it uses that you might reuse.
co_dispatched is the least obvious field and often the most useful. It lists the functions assigned together with this one in a module-level list, dict or tuple: route tables, handler maps, plugin registries. When you add another handler, it names the existing ones and so shows where they are registered, without reading the glue code.
The graph fields appear only when graph=True, the default for context. env_context and repo_context return content and metadata only.

title: skill
text:
The call graph
k.graph is the graph itself, a CodeGraph built from ast-grep static analysis plus Python AST rules for decorators, registrations and @patch. Besides the methods above it has k.graph.ranked(k=10, module='fastcore'), k.graph.callers, k.graph.file2nodes and k.graph.co_dispatched; doc(k.graph) lists them all.
Node names are the dotted mod_name from a hit’s metadata. A name that is not in the graph gives an empty result, not an error, so an empty short_path means either that there is no path or that a node is not indexed. Check k.ni(name) before concluding that two pieces of code do not connect.

title: skill
text:
Long-form docs
Code chunks suit code, not prose. k.docs is a separate index for READMEs and documentation folders, a litesearch Index that splits documents by heading. It is created the first time you use it:
k.add_pkg_docs('fastcore')          # a package's full README
k.add_docs('path/to/docs')          # a folder, a file, or {title: text}
k.docs_context('how do I install')  # ranked sections, each with a node_id
k.docs.read(node_id)['text']        # one whole section
docs_context(q, sections=False) returns raw chunks instead. The docs index does not track staleness: adding a changed document again stores the new text but does not remove the old version.

title: skill
text:
Reranking
context, env_context, repo_context and pkg_context take rerank=True, which reorders the hits with a flashrank cross-encoder, a small model that scores each hit against the query. The first call downloads the model. Reranking reorders what was retrieved and never adds to it.
It is off by default. It helps most when the query uses the same words as the target’s docstring. When a query is phrased differently, the right code is usually missing from the candidates in the first place, and reordering cannot bring it back. context reranks only its final top hits; env_context and repo_context first retrieve a wider pool for the reranker to choose from.

title: skill
text:
Outside Python
The same index can be reached in three other ways, for callers that are not Python processes:

Command line: kosha sync, kosha context 'query' --limit 10 --rerank, kosha ni <mod_name>, kosha public-api <pkg>, and --as-json on any of them for JSON output.
Daemon: kosha daemon keeps one embedding model loaded and reads {"cmd": ..., "args": {...}} requests as JSON lines on standard input, which saves the few seconds of loading on every call.
MCP: kosha-mcp offers the same operations as MCP tools over stdio. If the host already has it configured, call those tools instead of importing anything.

title: skill
text:
The indexes are litesearch databases
k.codedb and k.envdb are litesearch databases, so the whole litesearch API works on them: extra tables, raw SQL, custom stores.
list(k.envdb.q("select content from store where json_extract(metadata,'$.mod_name') = ?", ['fastcore.basics.merge']))
summaries = k.envdb.get_store(name='summaries')   # for example, notes an agent writes about undocumented code
Embeddings are stored and read back as 16-bit floats. kosha.core.cast_emb enforces that, so a custom embedding function cannot write a wider type by mistake.

from pyskills import doc, xdir, list_pyskills
import kosha.skill

# the entry point resolves, and its blurb is the first paragraph of the module docstring
assert 'kosha.skill' in list_pyskills(), list_pyskills().keys()
assert set(xdir(kosha.skill)) >= {'Kosha', 'CodeGraph', 'pkg_url'}  # plus the sibling submodules pyskills adds
print(list_pyskills()['kosha.skill'])

Search your repo and every installed package by meaning, then follow the call graph between them. Use it before you grep, open a source file, or write code a dependency already provides. Keyword search, vector search and a static call graph over local SQLite, with no LLM calls and no network.



# Every method the docstring names exists, so a host that follows it cannot raise AttributeError.
named = ['status','sync','context','env_context','repo_context','pkg_context','docs_context','public_api',
         'top_nodes','api_call_paths','dep_stack','where_to_add','ni','neighbors','short_path','add_docs','add_pkg_docs']
missing = [m for m in named if not hasattr(Kosha, m)]
assert not missing, f'skill docstring names methods Kosha does not have: {missing}'
gmissing = [m for m in ['ranked','callers','callees','co_dispatched','file2nodes','node_info'] if not hasattr(CodeGraph, m)]
assert not gmissing, gmissing
doc(kosha.skill)

title: cli
text:
This module provides one kosha command, for agents that work through a shell and for people at a terminal. Each query has a subcommand: sync, status, context, repo-context, env-context, ni, public-api, api-paths, dep-stack, top-nodes, where-to-add, watch, daemon, install, nuke, embed and prune. Subcommand names and flags use hyphens where the Python methods use underscores, as in --as-json and --busy-timeout. A flag that is on by default turns off with --no- in front, as in kosha sync --no-graph.
Output is readable markdown. --as-json prints JSON instead, for piping into jq or another program. kosha <subcommand> --help lists a subcommand’s flags.

from fastcore.foundation import L


assert _to_json({'a': {1, 2}}) == {'a': [1, 2]}
assert _to_json(L([{'x': 1}])) == [{'x': 1}]
assert _to_json('plain') == 'plain'
print("helpers ok")

helpers ok


kosha sync brings the index up to date, with the same switches as Kosha.sync: --no-repo, --no-env and --no-graph skip a part, --pkgs names the packages to index as a comma-separated list, and --force re-reads everything. To index packages in parallel, pass both --pkg-parallel and --busy-timeout 30000. When it finishes it prints the index status.



sync
def sync(
    dir:str=None, # directory to sync; defaults to repo root
    pkgs:str=None, # comma-separated package names; defaults to all pyproject.toml deps
    repo:bool=True, # index the repo
    env:bool=True, # index installed packages; --no-env indexes the repo only
    graph:bool=True, # build the call graph
    graph_mode:str='fast', # 'full' re-extracts changed files in worker processes
    graph_metrics:bool=True, # recompute PageRank after the graph update
    parallel:bool=True, # run repo, env, and graph sync in parallel
    embed:bool=True, # compute embeddings; --no-embed stores chunks for keyword search only
    force:bool=False, # re-sync everything, graph included, rather than what changed
    busy_timeout:int=None, # ms to wait on a locked db; set (e.g. 30000) when syncing in parallel
    pkg_parallel:bool=False, # index packages in parallel threads; needs --busy-timeout
    as_json:bool=False, # output the post-sync status as JSON
):
Index the repo, the installed packages and the call graph, then print the index status.



from fastcore.test import test_eq

test_eq(_split_pkgs('fastcore,httpx'), ['fastcore', 'httpx'])
# commas inside extras belong to the extras, not to the list
test_eq(_split_pkgs('rishi[litert,llama,all]'), ['rishi'])
test_eq(_split_pkgs('rishi[litert,llama,all],fastcore'), ['rishi', 'fastcore'])
test_eq(_split_pkgs('rishi[all]>=0.2, fastcore'), ['rishi>=0.2', ' fastcore'])
# empty segments would crash `_pkg_name`, so they never make it out
test_eq(_split_pkgs('fastcore,,'), ['fastcore'])
print('_split_pkgs tests passed')

_split_pkgs tests passed


kosha context "query" runs Kosha.context, the combined search over the repo and the packages, and prints each hit with its name, line, PageRank, the first 300 characters of its source and up to five callers. The query can carry key:value filters. A filter-shaped token with an unknown key, such as libr:litesearch, prints a warning on standard error. kosha searches that token as text and does not filter with it. repo-context and env-context search one index only.



context
def context(
    query:str, # search query (supports key:value filters e.g. package:fastcore)
    limit:int=10, # max results
    repo:bool=True, # include repo results
    env:bool=True, # include env results
    graph:bool=True, # include call graph enrichment
    rerank:bool=False, # reorder the top-k with a flashrank cross-encoder
    as_json:bool=False, # output JSON instead of markdown
):
Search the repo and installed packages together and print the hits with their call-graph details.



assert callable(sync)
assert callable(context)
print("sync + context defined ok")

# `sync` and `context` use the same flag names `repo`, `env` and `graph`.
# `sync` has no `--sync_graph` flag. The call graph is on by default, so `ni` and `where-to-add` have a graph to read.
from fastcore.script import anno_parser
_flags = {a.dest for a in anno_parser(sync, prog='kosha sync')._actions}
assert {'repo', 'env', 'graph', 'graph_mode', 'graph_metrics'} <= _flags, sorted(_flags)
assert 'sync_graph' not in _flags, sorted(_flags)
_ctx = {a.dest for a in anno_parser(context, prog='kosha context')._actions}
assert {'repo', 'env', 'graph'} <= _ctx, sorted(_ctx)

# `sync` passes `graph_mode` and `graph_metrics` to `Kosha.sync` unchanged.
_cli_calls = []
class _CliKosha:
    def __init__(self, **kwargs): pass
    def sync(self, **kwargs): _cli_calls.append(kwargs)
    def status(self): return {}
_cli_kosha, sync.__wrapped__.__globals__['Kosha'] = sync.__wrapped__.__globals__['Kosha'], _CliKosha
try: sync(graph_mode='full', graph_metrics=False)
finally: sync.__wrapped__.__globals__['Kosha'] = _cli_kosha
test_eq((_cli_calls[0]['graph_mode'], _cli_calls[0]['graph_metrics']), ('full', False))

sync + context defined ok






repo_context
def repo_context(
    query:str, # search query
    limit:int=10, # max results
    as_json:bool=False, # output JSON
):
Search the repo index only and print the hits.





env_context
def env_context(
    query:str, # search query (supports key:value filters e.g. package:fastcore)
    limit:int=10, # max results
    as_json:bool=False, # output JSON
):
Search the installed-package index only and print the hits.


The graph subcommands take full dotted names. kosha ni fastcore.basics.merge prints a node’s PageRank and up to ten of its callers, callees and co-dispatched peers. public-api, api-paths, dep-stack and top-nodes print the results of the Kosha methods of those names; dep-stack with no --seeds starts from the packages in pyproject.toml. kosha watch re-indexes files as they change, until Ctrl-C.



ni
def ni(
    mod_name:str, # full dotted node name, e.g. fastcore.basics.merge
    as_json:bool=False, # output JSON
):
Print the PageRank, callers, callees and co-dispatched peers of one graph node.





watch
def watch(
    dir:str=None, # directory to watch; defaults to repo root
):
Watch the repo and re-index files as they change, until Ctrl-C.





public_api
def public_api(
    pkg:str, # package name e.g. "fastcore" or submodule "fastcore.basics"
    module:str=None, # restrict to a submodule (overrides pkg for scoping)
    as_json:bool=False, # output JSON
):
Print the public names of a package or module, including functions @patch adds to its classes.





api_paths
def api_paths(
    from_pkg:str, # source package (call origin)
    to_pkg:str, # target package (call destination)
    k:int=15, # top-k API nodes per package to consider
    as_json:bool=False, # output JSON
):
Print the shortest call paths from the top public functions of from_pkg to those of to_pkg.





dep_stack
def dep_stack(
    seeds:str=None, # comma-separated seed package names; defaults to pyproject.toml deps
    depth:int=1, # number of layers below the seeds
    as_json:bool=False, # output JSON
):
Print the layers of packages imported by the seed packages, breadth first.





top_nodes
def top_nodes(
    pkg:str, # package name e.g. "fastcore"
    k:int=5, # number of top nodes to return
    as_json:bool=False, # output JSON
):
Print the k public names of a package with the highest PageRank.





status
def status(
    as_json:bool=False
):
Print how fresh the index is: file, package and node counts, stale files and stale packages.


kosha where-to-add "description" prints path:line suggestions for where new code should go, with the peers it would join. kosha nuke deletes the repo’s index and call graph, and kosha nuke --env also deletes the shared package and docs indexes.



where_to_add
def where_to_add(
    description:str, # what you want to add
    limit:int=5, # max results
    as_json:bool=False, # output JSON
):
Print the files and lines where code matching description would best be added.





nuke
def nuke(
    env:bool=False, # also delete the shared package and docs indexes
):
Delete the repo index and call graph, and with –env the shared indexes too.


kosha embed embeds the package chunks that sync --no-embed or an older kosha stored without an embedding. It works one batch at a time. Stopping it loses at most one batch. kosha prune removes the packages and versions that no indexed environment still has installed and compacts the index; --dry-run lists them without removing anything.



prune
def prune(
    dry_run:bool=False, # list what would be removed without removing it
    as_json:bool=False, # output JSON
):
Remove the packages and versions no indexed environment still has installed, and print what was removed.





embed
def embed(
    pkg:str=None, # only this package; defaults to every package
    batch:int=5000, # chunks embedded, committed and indexed together
):
Embed the package chunks that have no embedding yet and print how many were embedded.


kosha daemon keeps one Kosha loaded. Repeated queries then skip the few seconds that loading the embedding model takes. It prints {"ok": true, "status": "ready"}. It then reads one JSON request per line from standard input, such as {"cmd": "context", "args": {"q": "embed a query"}}, and writes one JSON line per answer: {"ok": true, "result": ...} or {"ok": false, "error": "..."}. The commands are the keys of _DISPATCH below, and their arguments are those of the Kosha methods of the same names. kosha install copies SKILL.md into the repository for coding agents.



daemon
def daemon():
Answer JSON requests from stdin, one per line, with one JSON line each on stdout, keeping kosha loaded.





install
def install():
Copy the bundled SKILL.md into .agents/skills/kosha/ and .claude/skills/kosha/ in the repo.


main is the entry point behind the kosha command. It looks up the subcommand in CMDS, parses the remaining arguments against that function’s signature, and calls it. With no subcommand, or an unknown one, it prints the list of subcommands.



main
def main():
Entry point for the kosha CLI command.



assert set(CMDS.keys()) == {
    'sync', 'context', 'repo-context', 'env-context', 'ni',
    'watch', 'public-api', 'api-paths', 'dep-stack', 'top-nodes',
    'daemon', 'status', 'where-to-add', 'install', 'nuke', 'embed', 'prune'
}
print(f"CMDS registered: {sorted(CMDS)}")

CMDS registered: ['api-paths', 'context', 'daemon', 'dep-stack', 'env-context', 'install', 'ni', 'public-api', 'repo-context', 'status', 'sync', 'top-nodes', 'watch', 'where-to-add']

title: refactor
refactor
refactor
text:
Text replacement
replace_plan(paths, query, replacement) is find and replace across files. The search is literal and case-insensitive by default. regex=True treats query as a regular expression, and replacement can then refer to groups. case=True makes the match case-sensitive. word=True matches whole words only, so koshas stays unchanged in the example below. The function returns a list of FileEdit objects for the changed files, and a list of skipped paths. It raises ValueError when query is empty, when the regular expression is invalid, or when the replacement is invalid.
replace_plan takes a list of paths and a read function, not a directory. read can return the text of files on disk, of a git revision, or of an editor’s unsaved buffers. replace_plan skips notebooks. It also skips a file that read cannot read, and a file whose text holds the Unicode replacement character. A binary file read as text holds that character.



replace_plan
def replace_plan(
    paths, query, replacement, regex:bool=False, case:bool=False, word:bool=False, read:function=_read
):
Plan one find-and-replace across paths: the changed files as FileEdits, and the paths skipped.



with TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    root = _tree(d, {'a.py': 'kosha = 1\nprint(koshas)\n', 'b.py': 'x = 2\n', 'nb.ipynb': '{}'})
    rows, skipped = replace_plan(sorted(root.iterdir()), 'kosha', 'kosha2', word=True)
    print([Path(r.path).name for r in rows], [Path(p).name for p in skipped])
    print(rows[0].after)

['a.py'] ['nb.ipynb']
kosha2 = 1
print(koshas)

title: refactor
text:
Symbols and their spans
The planners cut and paste text by character position. Python’s ast module reports a position as a line number and a column. The column counts UTF-8 bytes, not characters. On a line with an accented letter, every column after that letter is too large as a character offset. The private helpers here convert positions to character offsets.
top_symbols lists the top-level functions and classes of a file. Each entry holds the name, the kind, the line and the span of text that the definition owns. A definition owns more than its own lines. It owns its decorators, the comment block directly above it, and the blank lines below it. Removing the span leaves no gap. The example shows sep with its comment and its @cache decorator.



top_symbols
def top_symbols(
    source
):
Top-level functions and classes, each with the character span it owns.



SRC = '''import os

# the separator, repeated
@cache
def sep(n): return os.sep * n


class Thing:
    def go(self): return sep(1)
'''
top_symbols(SRC)

[{'name': 'sep', 'kind': 'function', 'line': 5, 'start': 11, 'end': 76},
 {'name': 'Thing', 'kind': 'class', 'line': 8, 'start': 76, 'end': 121}]



sym = top_symbols(SRC)[0]
print(SRC[sym['start']:sym['end']])

# the separator, repeated
@cache
def sep(n): return os.sep * n

title: refactor
section: Naming the module a file is
text:
Naming the module a file is
module_of turns a file path into the dotted module name that an import uses. It finds the import root of the file with kosha.core.imp_root. The index uses the same rule for mod_name, and the two names agree. The __init__.py of a package gives the package name, pkg, and not pkg.__init__.



module_of
def module_of(
    path
):
Dotted module name for a file, from the top of its __init__.py chain.



with TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    root = _tree(d, {'pkg/__init__.py': '', 'pkg/sub/__init__.py': '', 'pkg/sub/deep.py': '', 'loose.py': ''})
    print([module_of(root/p) for p in ('pkg/sub/deep.py', 'pkg/__init__.py', 'loose.py')])

['pkg.sub.deep', 'pkg', 'loose']

title: refactor
text:
Free names
Moved code works only if every name that it reads but does not define is available in the new file. These names are the free names of the code. In the example, the function reads BASE and os from its module. The file that receives the function must provide both. len is not free because it is a builtin. n and total are not free because the function defines them.
_free excludes the builtins by default. A module that defines its own filter or id must not exclude them. Otherwise the check treats a call to the filter of that module as satisfied by the builtin. move_plan handles that case, shown further down.

_body = ast.parse('def f(n):\n    total = BASE\n    return len(total) + n + os.sep\n').body
print(sorted(_free(_body)), '|', sorted(_free(_body, exclude=()) & {'len'}))

['BASE', 'os'] | ['len']

title: refactor
text:
Extract
extract(path, source, start, end, kind, name) takes the text between the character offsets start and end of source and moves it into a new definition called name. kind has four values:

'function': the selected statements become a function defined at the position of the selection, followed by a call to it. The selection must be whole statement lines.
'method': the same, but the new method goes into the class, after the method that held the selection. The call is self.name(...). The selection must be inside a method.
'variable': the selected expression is assigned to name on the line above, and name replaces the expression.
'constant': a literal value at module level becomes a constant. extract converts name to upper case. It puts the constant after the docstring and the import lines that follow it.

extract raises ValueError with the reason when it cannot lift the selection. It refuses an empty selection, a selection that is not whole statements (function, method) or not one expression (variable, constant), a selection that returns or yields, an invalid name, an unknown kind, a constant that is not a literal, and a constant outside module scope. A return or yield would change meaning inside a new function.



extract
def extract(
    path, source, start, end, kind, name
):
Plan lifting the selection start:end of source into a new function, method, variable or constant called name.


The new function’s parameters are the names the selection reads before it assigns them. Its return values are the names it assigns that the code after the selection still reads. Everything else stays local to the new function. Here rows becomes a parameter and total, which print reads afterwards, comes back as the return value.

F = '''def report(rows):
    total = 0
    for r in rows: total += r

'''

title: refactor
text:
Inline
inline(path, source, pos) is the reverse of extracting a variable. Put pos on a use of a variable. The variable must have exactly one assignment, written as a plain name = value on lines of its own. inline replaces every use of the variable with the value and deletes the assignment. It wraps a value in parentheses unless the value is a name, constant, attribute, subscript, call, list, dict, set, comprehension or f-string. A tuple value gets parentheses. width = 1 + 2 inlined into width * 3 gives (1 + 2) * 3, not 1 + 2 * 3.
inline raises ValueError when pos is not on a variable, or when the variable is assigned more than once, declared global or nonlocal, never read, or read before the assignment. It also raises ValueError when the assignment shares its lines with other code.
inline refuses a substitution it cannot show to be safe, because it does not resolve scopes. The variable’s name must be bound nowhere else in the file, not even as a parameter. A value that reads other names needs every use in the assignment’s own scope, and each of those names bound once and before the assignment. A value that calls something, reads an attribute or item, builds a list, dict or set, or applies an operator, comparison or f-string to a name can run only once. inline accepts it only for a single use in the very next statement, outside any lambda, comprehension or conditional expression, outside the later operands of a chained comparison, and with no other call evaluated first.



inline
def inline(
    path, source, pos
):
Replace a variable’s uses with its value and delete the assignment.



I = 'width = 1 + 2\nprint(width * 3, width)\n'
inline('i.py', I, I.index('width')).after

'print((1 + 2) * 3, (1 + 2))\n'

text:
Imports
When a move adds an import, the import is relative if the importing module and the target share a package. Inside pkg.c, the module pkg.b is imported as from .b import .... Modules with no shared package get an absolute import. Kosha resolves an existing relative import against the module that holds it. from .a import x inside pkg.c and from pkg.a import x inside pkg.d both import the module pkg.a.

print(_stmt('pkg.b', 'pkg.c', ['shared']))          # same package: relative
print(_stmt('other.b', 'pkg.c', ['shared']))        # nothing shared: absolute
print(_absolute(ast.parse('from .a import x').body[0], 'pkg.c'))

from .b import shared
from other.b import shared
pkg.a


A new import goes with the existing imports of the file. If the file already has a from import of the same module, the name is added to that import and the module is not repeated. A new import statement goes below the module docstring, the imports and the __all__ that an nbdev module starts with.

_t = '"doc"\nimport os\nfrom pkg.b import one\n\nprint(one)\n'
_p = _parse('c.py', _t)
print(_apply(_t, _add_imports(_t, _p, _starts(_t), 'pkg.c', {'pkg.b': {'two'}, 'pkg.d': {'three'}}, {'import sys'})))

title: refactor
text:
Moving a definition
A move must also keep the __all__ of each module correct. __all__ is the list of public names of a module. Kosha rewrites __all__ when it is a plain list or tuple of strings. The rewritten value is a list. Kosha adds the moved names to the __all__ of the destination. It removes them from the __all__ of the source when shim=False. Kosha leaves __all__ unchanged when the module builds it any other way, such as ['x'] + more. A rewrite would need a guess.
Every file that imported a moved name must import it from the destination module. _repoint changes two kinds of import.

from src import name: Kosha splits the statement. The names that stayed keep the old import, and the moved names get a new import from the destination.
import src, used as src.name: Kosha replaces each src.name with name and adds a direct import of name. It removes import src, or src from a longer import statement, only when nothing else in the file uses src.

In the second kind, Kosha leaves the src.name uses unchanged when the file already binds name at its top level. Kosha adds a note in that case. A rewrite would point the uses at the wrong definition.
move_plan(src, names, dest, others) combines these steps. It cuts the named top-level functions and classes out of src, with the comments and decorators that they own. It appends them to dest, and creates dest if it does not exist. It copies the imports that the moved code needs into dest. It imports the names that the moved code reads from src itself back from src. By default src keeps a re-export: an import of the moved names from dest. Code that still imports the names from src keeps working. shim=False leaves the re-export out. move_plan also changes the imports of the names in every file of others, as described above.
Before it returns, move_plan checks every file in the plan for names that the edit would leave undefined. If it finds any, it raises ValueError with the file and the names. It returns a tuple of the plan and a list of notes. The notes describe things that move_plan did not do, such as a re-export that it left out.



move_plan
def move_plan(
    src, names, dest, others:tuple=(), shim:bool=True, read:function=_read
):
Plan moving top-level definitions names from src into dest and repointing the imports in others.



A move, end to end
The example project has three files in the package pkg. a.py defines shared. b.py is the destination. c.py imports shared by name. show prints each file of the plan as it would be after the move.

PROJECT = {'pkg/__init__.py': '',
           'pkg/a.py': '''
                "paths"
                import os

                def helper(x): return x + 1

                # the separator, repeated
                def shared(n): return os.sep * n
                ''',
           'pkg/b.py': '"where shared is going"\n',
           'pkg/c.py': 'from pkg.a import helper, shared\n\nprint(shared(2), helper(1))\n'}

def show(rows, notes=()):
    for r in rows: print(f'==== {Path(r.path).name} ' + ('(new) ' if r.before is None else '') + '='*20); print(r.after)
    for n in notes: print('note:', n)


with TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    root = _tree(d, PROJECT)
    rows, notes = move_plan(root/'pkg/a.py', ['shared'], root/'pkg/b.py', others=[root/'pkg/c.py'])
    show(rows, notes)

==== a.py ====================
"paths"
import os
from .b import shared

def helper(x): return x + 1

==== b.py ====================
"where shared is going"
import os


# the separator, repeated
def shared(n): return os.sep * n

==== c.py ====================
from pkg.a import helper
from .b import shared

print(shared(2), helper(1))



a.py keeps a re-export. Code that imported shared from a.py still works. With shim=False, a.py has no re-export. Only the files in others keep working.

with TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    root = _tree(d, PROJECT)
    rows, notes = move_plan(root/'pkg/a.py', ['shared'], root/'pkg/b.py', others=[root/'pkg/c.py'], shim=False)
    print(rows[0].after)

"paths"
import os

def helper(x): return x + 1





The hard cases
c.py uses import pkg.a and reaches the moved function as pkg.a.shared. That use becomes a direct import of shared from pkg.b. The import pkg.a line stays because c.py still reads pkg.a.helper. e.py imports the module under an alias. f.py imports shared with a relative import. move_plan changes both files as well.

with TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    root = _tree(d, dict(PROJECT, **{'pkg/c.py': 'import pkg.a\n\nprint(pkg.a.shared(2), pkg.a.helper(1))\n',
                                     'pkg/e.py': 'import pkg.a as pa\n\nprint(pa.shared(2))\n',
                                     'pkg/f.py': 'from .a import shared\n\nprint(shared(2))\n'}))
    others = [root/'pkg/c.py', root/'pkg/e.py', root/'pkg/f.py']
    rows, notes = move_plan(root/'pkg/a.py', ['shared'], root/'pkg/b.py', others=others)
    show(rows[2:], notes)

==== c.py ====================
import pkg.a
from .b import shared

print(shared(2), pkg.a.helper(1))

==== e.py ====================
from .b import shared

print(shared(2))

==== f.py ====================
from .b import shared

print(shared(2))



A definition can have the same name as a builtin, and a check that ignores builtins goes wrong on it. a.py defines filter, and use calls it. When filter moves out of a.py, a.py must import it from the destination. A check that ignored builtins would decide that filter is always available. It would skip the import, and use would call the builtin filter. move_plan adds the import.

SHADOW = {'pkg/__init__.py': '',
          'pkg/a.py': 'def filter(xs): return [x for x in xs if x]\n\ndef use(xs): return len(filter(xs))\n',
          'pkg/b.py': '"where filter is going"\n'}

with TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    root = _tree(d, SHADOW)
    rows, notes = move_plan(root/'pkg/a.py', ['filter'], root/'pkg/b.py', shim=False)
    print(rows[0].after)

from .b import filter

def use(xs): return len(filter(xs))



move_plan refuses a move that would make two modules import each other. Here the moved shared reads BASE from a.py. helper stays in a.py and calls shared. After the move, b.py would import BASE from a.py, and a.py would import shared from b.py. The ValueError tells you to move BASE as well.

CIRCULAR = {'pkg/__init__.py': '',
            'pkg/a.py': 'BASE = 3\n\ndef shared(n): return BASE * n\n\ndef helper(x): return shared(x) + 1\n',
            'pkg/b.py': '"b"\n'}

with TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    root = _tree(d, CIRCULAR)
    test_fail(lambda: move_plan(root/'pkg/a.py', ['shared'], root/'pkg/b.py'),
              contains='pkg.a and pkg.b would import each other over BASE')
    print('refused')

refused


If nothing left in a.py uses the moved definition, there is no real cycle. b.py still imports BASE from a.py. move_plan leaves the re-export out of a.py and adds a note.

with TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    root = _tree(d, dict(CIRCULAR, **{'pkg/a.py': 'BASE = 3\n\ndef shared(n): return BASE * n\n\ndef helper(x): return x + 1\n'}))
    rows, notes = move_plan(root/'pkg/a.py', ['shared'], root/'pkg/b.py')
    show(rows, notes)

==== a.py ====================
BASE = 3

def helper(x): return x + 1

==== b.py ====================
"b"
from .a import BASE


def shared(n): return BASE * n

note: re-export left out: pkg.b imports BASE back from pkg.a


Several definitions can move at once. They keep their order from the source file. A class moves with all its methods. With shim=False, move_plan updates __all__ in both files.

MANY = {'pkg/__init__.py': '',
        'pkg/a.py': "__all__ = ['helper', 'shared', 'Thing']\nimport os\n\n"
                    "def helper(x): return x + 1\n\ndef shared(n): return os.sep * n\n\n"
                    "class Thing:\n    def go(self): return shared(1)\n",
        'pkg/b.py': "__all__ = ['already']\n\ndef already(): pass\n"}

with TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    root = _tree(d, MANY)
    rows, notes = move_plan(root/'pkg/a.py', ['shared', 'Thing'], root/'pkg/b.py', shim=False)
    show(rows, notes)

==== a.py ====================
__all__ = ['helper']
import os

def helper(x): return x + 1

==== b.py ====================
__all__ = ['already', 'shared', 'Thing']
import os

def already(): pass


def shared(n): return os.sep * n

class Thing:
    def go(self): return shared(1)



Each refusal raises ValueError with a message that states the problem. Most messages also name the file. The tests below check the messages.

title: kosha
text:
Find the code you need before you write it.

kosha (कोश, “treasury”) keeps a searchable index of your repository and of the Python packages it depends on. Ask it in plain words, such as “atomic write to a temp file”, and it returns the functions and classes that do that, from your code and from your dependencies, with their file, line and source. Ask it about a function and it tells you what calls it, what it calls, and how much code depends on it. This shows what a change will touch.
kosha serves coding agents and people. An agent that searches before it writes reuses the helper your project already has instead of adding a second one. kosha runs locally, uses no language model, and returns real code you can read.
This page uses three terms. A chunk is one function, class or method cut out of a source file and stored with its metadata. The index finds chunks with two searches at once. Keyword search matches the words of the query. Vector search compares embeddings. An embedding is a list of numbers computed from text, and code with similar meaning gets similar numbers. The call graph records which function uses which, across your code and your packages.


kosha is a development tool, so add it as a dev dependency. The package is published as koshas; the module you import and the command you run are both kosha.
uv add --dev koshas
The package includes a skill file, SKILL.md, that tells coding agents how to use kosha. Install it once per project:
Kosha(install_skill=True)   # writes .agents/skills/kosha/SKILL.md and .claude/skills/kosha/SKILL.md
Commit .agents/skills/kosha/SKILL.md so that every contributor’s agent picks it up.



Kosha() opens the index for the repository you are in. sync() brings it up to date: it indexes your repo files, the packages listed in pyproject.toml with their direct dependencies, and the call graph between them. The first sync takes a while. Later syncs re-read only files and package versions that changed.
k = Kosha()
k.sync()
k.sync(graph=False) skips the call graph when you only need search. graph_mode='full' re-extracts the graph in worker processes. graph_metrics=False skips recomputing PageRank, which is defined below. Call k.graph.recompute_metrics() after your last update. The example below syncs only two packages.

k = Kosha()
k.sync(pkgs=['fastcore', 'litesearch'])

status tells you whether the index is current. stale_files counts repo files changed since they were indexed, new_files counts Python files not indexed yet, and stale_pkgs lists installed packages not yet indexed at their installed version. Run k.sync() again after uv add, an upgrade, or a large edit, or whenever these are not zero.
k.sync(embed=False) is a faster sync that stores new chunks without embeddings. Keyword search finds them straight away, and k.process_repo() and k.process_env() add the embeddings later.



env_context searches the installed packages. Searching them first often turns up a function that already does what you were about to write. Here a search for an atomic file write finds fsspec.utils.atomic_write and a Jupyter helper among others. Each hit is a dict with the chunk’s content and its metadata, which includes the dotted name (mod_name), the file path and the line number.

results = k.env_context('atomic write temp file permissions', limit=5)
for r in results:
    print(r['metadata']['mod_name'])
    print(' ', r['content'].splitlines()[0])
    print()

Filters narrow a search. Write them in the query as key:value: package: for an installed package, path: and file: for a path glob, lang: for a language, and type: for the kind of definition, such as FunctionDef. Each filter excludes everything that does not match. A trailing !, as in package!:fastcore, means the same as without it.
A package name written as a plain word behaves differently in context, the combined search below. It only raises that package’s hits, and other packages still appear.
k.env_context('package:fastcore path:xtras atomic save', limit=8)   # only fastcore, only paths containing xtras
k.context('fastcore atomic save', limit=8)                          # fastcore ranked higher, others still listed
When a hit comes from a package you do not know, pkg_url gives the address of its repository or home page, which you can hand to a web search for its documentation or changelog:

from kosha.core import pkg_url
pkg_url('litesearch')

context is the search to reach for first. It searches your repo and the packages at once, merges the two lists, and reorders the hits with rules made for code: a query that names a symbol favours the chunk that defines it, and test files and re-exports rank lower. With graph=True each hit also carries its place in the call graph: pagerank, callers, callees and co_dispatched.

results = k.context('search code embeddings', limit=6, graph=True)
for r in results:
    m = r['metadata']
    print(f"{m['mod_name']}  L{m.get('lineno','?')}  "
          f"pr={r.get('pagerank') or 0:.4f}  callers={list(r.get('callers',[]))[:2]}")

PageRank, the algorithm Google first used to rank web pages, scores how much of the graph depends on a node. A function with a high score is called from many places, or from places that are themselves called a lot, so a change to it reaches further. Treat it as a warning to look before you edit. Most nodes score close to zero, as here.



ni (node info) takes a full dotted name and returns the node’s graph record: its PageRank, the functions that call it, the functions it calls, and its co-dispatched peers. Call it before you change a function. In this example fastcore.basics.merge is called from two places in fastcore.script.

info = k.ni('fastcore.basics.merge')
print('pagerank:', info.get('pagerank', 0))
print('callers: ', list(info.get('callers', []))[:5])
print('callees: ', list(info.get('callees', []))[:5])
print('co_dispatched:', list(info.get('co_dispatched', []))[:5])

co_dispatched lists the node’s peers: functions registered together, in a route list, a handler table or a list of plugins. When you add a new member to such a group, the peers show the pattern to copy.



where_to_add takes a description of new code and suggests where it should go. For each suggestion it gives the file, the line to insert after, and the node it would sit next to. When that node belongs to a co-dispatch group, the line is the end of the group’s last member in the file, so the new code lands beside its peers.

pts = k.where_to_add('add dynamic ast parsing for patched functions', limit=3)
for p in pts:
    co = ', '.join(p['co_dispatched'][:3])
    print(f"{p['path']}:{p['insert_after']}  ({p['node']})")
    if co: print(f'  peers: {co}')

Each new Python process pays three to five seconds to load the embedding model before its first search. kosha daemon loads it once and then answers requests read from standard input, one JSON object per line, writing one JSON line per answer. It prints {"ok": true, "status": "ready"} when it is ready.

Each request names a command and its arguments:
{"cmd": "context", "args": {"q": "embed a query", "limit": 10}}
{"ok": true, "result": [...]}

{"cmd": "short_path", "args": {"src": "kosha.core.Kosha.sync", "tgt": "litesearch.core.search"}}
{"ok": true, "result": [...]}
A failed request returns {"ok": false, "error": "..."}. The commands are sync, status, context, repo_context, env_context, ni, neighbors, short_path, top_nodes, public_api, api_call_paths, dep_stack, where_to_add and nuke, with the same arguments as the Kosha methods of those names. ni takes mod_name.

Kosha() opens the index for the repository you are in. sync() brings it up to date: it indexes your repo files, the packages listed in pyproject.toml with their direct dependencies, and the call graph between them. Each filter excludes everything that does not match. A trailing !, as in package!:fastcore, means the same as without it.
A package name written as a plain word behaves differently in context, the combined search below. It only raises that package’s hits, and other packages still appear.

context is the search to reach for first. It searches your repo and the packages at once, merges the two lists, and reorders the hits with rules made for code: a query that names a symbol favours the chunk that defines it, and test files and re-exports rank lower.     print(f"{m['mod_name']}  L{m.get('lineno','?')}  "
          f"pr={r.get('pagerank') or 0:.4f}  callers={list(r.get('callers',[]))[:2]}")

PageRank, the algorithm Google first used to rank web pages, scores how much of the graph depends on a node. A function with a high score is called from many places, or from places that are themselves called a lot, so a change to it reaches further. Treat it as a warning to look before you edit. Most nodes score close to zero, as here.

co_dispatched lists the node’s peers: functions registered together, in a route list, a handler table or a list of plugins. When you add a new member to such a group, the peers show the pattern to copy.

title: kosha
text:
where_to_add takes a description of new code and suggests where it should go. For each suggestion it gives the file, the line to insert after, and the node it would sit next to. When that node belongs to a co-dispatch group, the line is the end of the group’s last member in the file, so the new code lands beside its peers.

pts = k.where_to_add('add dynamic ast parsing for patched functions', limit=3)
for p in pts:
    co = ', '.join(p['co_dispatched'][:3])
    print(f"{p['path']}:{p['insert_after']}  ({p['node']})")
    if co: print(f'  peers: {co}')

title: core
text:
This module builds the index that shows whether your code or one of your dependencies already has a helper you need. It splits source files into chunks, one per function, class or method. It stores each chunk with its metadata and an embedding. An embedding is a vector of numbers computed from the code, and chunks with similar meaning have similar vectors. A search combines two methods. Keyword search (SQLite’s FTS5) finds chunks that contain the words of the query. Vector search finds chunks whose embedding is close to the query’s embedding. No language model is involved, and everything runs locally.
There are two indexes. The repo index covers your own code and lives in .kosha/code.db inside the repository. The package index covers installed packages and lives in your user data directory (~/.local/share/kosha/env.db on most systems). Every project on the machine shares it, and a package version is indexed once. The Kosha class owns both indexes. The graph module holds the call graph built from them.

title: core
text:
Utilities
These helpers support the indexing code below. Most users never call them directly.
parse reads Python source, from a string or a file path, and returns its syntax tree along with what kosha needs from it: a map from each imported name to its top-level package, the names of top-level functions and classes, the same plus module-level names assigned from a call, and a map from each imported name to its full dotted path. Results are cached, so calling it again on the same input is free. Source that does not parse gives None and empty collections.



parse
def parse(
    code:NoneType=None, p:NoneType=None
):
Parse code or the file p and return (tree, imports, top-level defs, defs plus call-assigned names, import paths).


The package includes a SKILL.md file that tells coding agents how to use kosha. mv_skill_md copies it to .agents/skills/kosha/SKILL.md and .claude/skills/kosha/SKILL.md in the repository, or under dir if you give one. By default it prints the target paths and copies nothing. Pass dry_run=False to write the files. Kosha(install_skill=True) and the kosha install command call it for you.



mv_skill_md

    dry_run:bool=True, dir:NoneType=None
)->None:
Copy the bundled SKILL.md into .agents/skills/kosha/ and .claude/skills/kosha/; dry_run only prints the targets.


arun runs a coroutine from ordinary code. asyncio.run fails inside a running event loop, and Jupyter notebook code runs inside one. In that case arun runs the coroutine in a worker thread with its own loop. arun returns the result wrapped in a fastcore L. The two tests below show both paths.



arun
def arun(
    coro
)-><built-in function any>:
Run coro to completion from synchronous code, even inside a running event loop, and return its result in an L.



async def _add(a, b): return a + b
assert arun(_add(1, 2)) == L(3)
print('arun: sync context ok')

arun: sync context ok



async def _test_nested():
    result = arun(_add(10, 20))
    assert first(result) == 30, f'got {result}'
arun(_test_nested())
print('arun: nested-loop context ok')

arun: nested-loop context ok



mv_skill_md()

To decide which packages to index, kosha starts from the dependencies listed in your pyproject.toml and follows their own requirements. pkg_trans_deps(seeds, depth) does the walk. It returns the seed packages plus the packages they require, depth levels down. It keeps only installed packages and skips optional extras. With depth=0 it returns the seeds.
env_pkg_versions returns {package name: installed version} for the packages to index. With pyproject=True, the default, it starts from the dependencies in pyproject.toml and expands depth levels with pkg_trans_deps. It returns an empty dict when there is no repository root or no pyproject.toml. With pyproject=False it returns every installed package. The examples show both.

    seeds:list, depth:int=2, path:list=None
)->fastcore.foundation.L:
The seeds plus the installed packages they require, depth levels down, ignoring optional extras.





env_path

    root
)->list:
The site-packages folders of the environment in root: its .venv, else $VIRTUAL_ENV when that lies inside root; empty when there is none.

)->list:
Names of the dependencies in root/pyproject.toml, plus the comma-separated xtras groups; None when root (default: the git repository of the current folder) has no such file.





env_pkg_versions
def env_pkg_versions(

)->dict:
{name: version} of the packages to index: the dependencies of the pyproject.toml in root expanded depth levels, or all installed packages.



installed_packages(pyproject=True)

title: core
text:
Kosha
Kosha is the object you work with. Create one in your repository with Kosha(). It finds the repository root, opens the repo index in .kosha/code.db and the shared package index in the user data directory, and loads the embedding model. Its arguments let you point it somewhere else: dir sets the repository root, xdg_dir the data directory that holds the package index, and efn the embedding model, by default litesearch’s static code embedder. install_skill=True also installs SKILL.md. Set busy_timeout (in milliseconds) when several processes or threads write to the index at once, as update_pkgs(parallel=True) does.
Inside, the object holds three stores: code_st for repo chunks, env_st for package chunks, and pkg_st for package descriptions. Four plain tables sit beside them. packages records each indexed package version, and pkg_deps and repo_deps count which packages each package or repo module imports. repo_file_imports keeps the packages each repo file imports, so an incremental update_repo recounts repo_deps without parsing unchanged files.
cast_emb makes sure every vector kosha stores has the data type the search code reads back (16-bit floats), whatever the embedding model returns.

    busy_timeout:int=None, # ms to wait for a locked database; set it for parallel indexing

Chunk names are dotted paths like fastcore.basics.merge. To build them, kosha needs a file’s import root: the directory a Python import starts from. has_init checks whether a directory is a package (it holds an __init__.py or a compiled __init__ module), and imp_root climbs from a file to the nearest ancestor that is not a package.

    p:pathlib.Path
)->pathlib.Path:
The directory imports of p start from: its nearest ancestor that is not a package.





has_init

    d:pathlib.Path
)->bool:
True if d is a Python package directory: it holds __init__.py or a compiled __init__*.so.


litesearch’s file_parse splits a file into chunks, one per top-level function, class or assignment. enrich_chunks prepares them for the index. It marks each chunk as public API or not. A name is public when it is in the module’s __all__, or, when the module has no __all__, when it has no leading underscore. It records the docstring. It adds every method of a class as a chunk of its own, so a search can return Table.insert_all and not only Table. enrich_chunks reads assignment chunks only to find __all__ and does not return them.



enrich_chunks
def enrich_chunks(
    content:fastcore.foundation.L
)->fastcore.foundation.L:
Mark chunks as public or private, record their docstrings, add one chunk per class method, and drop assignment chunks.

title: core
text:
Indexing packages
update_pkg indexes one installed package. It parses the package’s source files into chunks, stores them in the package index with an embedding, and records in pkg_deps how many of its modules import each other package. A package already indexed at its installed version is not parsed again, unless you pass force=True, but any of its chunks still without an embedding are embedded. update_pkgs does the same for a list. Use parallel=True to index several packages in threads at once; that needs a Kosha built with a busy_timeout, and without one it raises an error, as the test below shows. rm_pkg removes a package, or one version of it, from the index.
process_env computes embeddings for package chunks that were stored without one, for example after update_pkgs(embed=False); reembed=True recomputes all of them. It works through embed_missing, which does the same for any store and keeps its HNSW index in step. nuke deletes the repo’s .kosha directory, which holds the repo index and the call graph, and with env=True also the shared data directory holding the package and docs indexes. count_imp counts, for a list of files, how many import each top-level package.



count_imp
def count_imp(
    files, own:str=''
)->collections.Counter:
For a list of files, the number of files importing each top-level package other than own.





Kosha.process_env
def process_env(
    pkg:str=None, # only this package's chunks; None embeds every package
    reembed:bool=False, # embed chunks that already have an embedding too
    batch:int=5000, # chunks embedded, committed and indexed together
    progress:bool=False, # show a progress bar
)->int:
Embed package chunks and descriptions that have no embedding yet, or all of them with reembed=True, and return how many chunks were embedded.





embed_missing
def embed_missing(
    st, # hash-id store, HNSW-indexed or not
    emb_fn, # list of texts -> vectors
    where:str=None, # extra SQL condition on the rows
    where_args:dict=None, # named parameters for `where`
    reembed:bool=False, # embed rows that already have an embedding too
    batch:int=5000, # rows embedded, committed and indexed together
    progress:bool=False, # show a progress bar
)->int:
Embed the rows of st that have no embedding, batch at a time, adding each batch to the HNSW index; returns how many were embedded.





Kosha.nuke
def nuke(
    env:bool=False
):
Delete the repo index and call graph, and with env=True the shared package and docs indexes too.





Kosha.update_pkgs
def update_pkgs(
    pkgs:str | list=None, # package name or list of names to index; nothing happens if empty
    embed:bool=True, # embed chunks after indexing
    exts:str='.py,.js,.ts,.jsx,.tsx,.java,.go,.cs,.ruby,.php,.swift,.kt,.kts,.rs,.scala,.lua', # file extensions to include
    verbose:bool=True, # print progress
    force:bool=False, # reindex even if package version already loaded
    parallel:bool=False, # ingest packages concurrently; requires Kosha(busy_timeout=...)
    n_workers:NoneType=None, # threads when parallel=True; fastcore's default if None
    chunk:int=5000, # rows per write transaction when parallel=True
    **kwargs
):
Index each package in pkgs, in turn or in parallel threads.





Kosha.rm_pkg
def rm_pkg(
    pkg:str, ver:str=None
):
Remove package pkg, or only version ver, and its chunks from the index.





Kosha.update_pkg
def update_pkg(
    pkg:str, embed:bool=True,
    exts:str='.py,.js,.ts,.jsx,.tsx,.java,.go,.cs,.ruby,.php,.swift,.kt,.kts,.rs,.scala,.lua', verbose:bool=True,
    force:bool=False, imports:bool=False, chunk:int=5000, *, n_workers:int=None, threadpool:bool=False,
    path:list=None
):
Index installed package pkg: parse, store and embed its chunks, and record its imports and version.





Kosha.put_pkg_doc
def put_pkg_doc(
    pkg:str, embed:bool=True
)->dict:
Store the pkg_doc record of pkg in pkg_store, replacing older ones, and return it.



# update_pkgs(parallel=True) refuses without a busy timeout. Concurrent database() opens would hit
# apsw's 100ms default and raise SQLITE_BUSY inside the open hook. That drops whole packages and no
# exception reaches the caller. A silently incomplete index is worse than a loud failure.
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path
_gt = tempfile.mkdtemp(); _gk = Kosha(dir=_gt, xdg_dir=Path(_gt))
assert _gk.busy_timeout is None
try:
    _gk.update_pkgs(['certifi'], parallel=True, embed=False, verbose=False)
    assert False, 'parallel=True without busy_timeout must raise'
except ValueError as e: assert 'busy timeout' in str(e)
_gk.update_pkgs(['certifi'], parallel=False, embed=False, verbose=False)   # serial path is unguarded
assert len(_gk.env_st()) > 0

# with a timeout set, threaded ingestion must store exactly what the serial path stores
_pk = ['certifi', 'idna', 'fastlite']
_ta, _tb = tempfile.mkdtemp(), tempfile.mkdtemp()
_ka = Kosha(dir=_ta, xdg_dir=Path(_ta), busy_timeout=30_000)
_kb = Kosha(dir=_tb, xdg_dir=Path(_tb), busy_timeout=30_000)
_ka.update_pkgs(_pk, parallel=True,  embed=False, verbose=False)
_kb.update_pkgs(_pk, parallel=False, embed=False, verbose=False)
assert {r['name'] for r in _ka.pkgs(select='name')} == set(_pk), 'parallel lost a package'
assert len(_ka.env_st()) == len(_kb.env_st()), 'parallel dropped rows vs serial'

Kosha finds the project’s own environment once, in Kosha.env_path: the .venv in its root, else $VIRTUAL_ENV when that lies inside the root. kosha reads packages from that environment and not from the interpreter that runs kosha. A package installed only in the project’s .venv appears in status and update_pkg indexes it, with the version and file paths of that copy. When there is no such environment, env_path is empty and kosha uses the running interpreter.

from fastcore.test import test_eq

sync(embed=False) stores chunks for keyword search only. Indexing the same package again with embeddings on embeds those chunks too, even though the package is already loaded at its installed version. A first sync with embed=False does not leave the package invisible to vector search.

_et = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()); _er, _esp = _fake_proj(_et, 'proj')
_fake_dist(_esp, 'kkledger', '1.0', 'def parse_ledger(path): return open(path).read().split()\n\ndef sum_ledger(rows): return sum(map(float, rows))\n')
_ek = Kosha(dir=_er, xdg_dir=_et/'xdg')
_ek.update_pkg('kkledger', embed=False, verbose=False)
_nulls = lambda: (len(_ek.env_st(where="package='kkledger' AND embedding IS NULL")), len(_ek.pkg_st(where='embedding IS NULL')))
_unembedded = _nulls()
_ek.update_pkg('kkledger', verbose=False)
test_eq((_unembedded, _nulls()), ((2, 1), (0, 0)))
_unembedded, _nulls()

Chunks stored without an embedding before that behaviour existed need a backfill. process_env embeds every such chunk, batch at a time. It commits each batch and adds it to the HNSW index in the same step. An interrupted backfill resumes where it stopped. Vector search sees each chunk as soon as the chunk has a vector:

_fake_dist(_esp, 'kkinvoice', '2.0', 'def render_invoice(order): return f"Invoice {order}"\n\ndef email_invoice(addr, pdf): pass\n\ndef void_invoice(n): return -n\n')
_ek.update_pkg('kkinvoice', embed=False, verbose=False)
_idx = lambda: _ek.envdb.get_index(_ek.env_st.name)
_size = _idx().size
_done = _ek.process_env(batch=2)
test_eq((_done, _idx().size - _size, len(_ek.env_st(where='embedding IS NULL'))), (3, 3, 0))
_nearest(_ek, 'render an invoice for an order')

title: core
text:
Indexing the repository
update_repo indexes your own code. It walks the repository, skipping folders whose names start with . or _ and the build and dist folders, and skipping files whose names start with . or _ as well as setup.py and conftest.py. It compares each file’s modification time with the time recorded at the last run. It re-parses only files that are new or changed, and deletes chunks of files that are gone. Every project on the machine shares the package index. The index can therefore hold packages that no environment has any more, such as a dependency you removed or every package of a project folder you deleted. prune_env removes them. It judges what is installed by the *.dist-info folders in each site-packages folder it knows. It lists folders and never imports a package. It knows these folders: the folders the indexed chunks were read from, the nearest .venv above an editable install’s source, and the current project’s environment. A folder that no longer exists holds nothing.
A package keeps its chunks while any of those folders holds it at any version. A package has one set of chunks in the index, from whichever version was synced last. A chunk’s version records the version at which the chunk was first stored. An unchanged function from an old release is still current code. A chunk’s version does not identify stale chunks. Each packages row, one per indexed version, stays while some folder holds that exact version. Removing a package also drops its description and import counts. prune_env then runs VACUUM once to shrink the file. After that it rebuilds the chunk index and the package-description index once each. Each of these two indexes is an approximate nearest-neighbour index of the HNSW kind.
